One

Raising an order

What the office types in, and everything built from it.

Each part and product is described once. This one is a unit we sell.

The steps it travels through, in order, with what to do at each one.

And what it is built from. Each part is tied to the step that consumes it.

Raising the order. The drawing that came with the purchase order goes on here too.

The first thing it says is that a part is missing. Nothing can be built until it lands.

So it will not promise a finish date. It says how much work there is instead.

One press created five steps and a sub-assembly order of its own.

Two

On the floor

What a worker sees, and what gets recorded while they work.

A worker signs in and picks the machine they are standing at.

Their job: what to build, what to do, and what to fetch before starting.

Material is never assumed. They scan the label on the pallet they lifted.

That scan moves the stock, and ties this heat number to this job for good.

Only now will the clock start. With the steel still on the rack, it would not.

One is cut wrong. Scrap is two presses, and it asks why.

The steel is written off against that reason, and the job asks for a replacement.

Signed off, and still reachable for the rest of the shift in case of a mistake.

Nobody filled a timesheet in. Clock time and time charged to the job stay apart.

Every write-off lands here with its reason, its quantity, and who recorded it.

Three

Stock

Where material comes from, where it goes, and when to buy more.

What is on the racks, what is free, and what is already promised to jobs.

Every batch carries its own barcode, its heat number, and where it sits.

Booking the late insulation in. The heat number is what makes it traceable.

The label prints straight away. That barcode is what the floor scans.

The shortage cleared itself, and the order now has a date it can stand behind.

Four

Being told

Nobody should have to go looking for a problem.

A supervisor puts a name on a job, at the machine, without a dropdown.

That person is told by name, on the first screen they see.

Their alerts. Only what concerns them, not the whole floor.

A supervisor's: work that can now start, and steel to reorder before it runs out.

And the question this whole thing exists to answer: what is held up, and on what.

Five

Out of the door

A finished unit becomes stock, and stock goes on a truck.

Every step signed off by the person who did it, with what it actually took.

Signing off the last step puts the unit on the rack, under its own order number.

The driver's screen: built, and waiting for a truck.

One press raises the delivery note and takes it off the rack.

And the office can see it has gone, without ringing anyone to ask.

Thermal Corp MES
